content_voiceover: This chelator table is a board favorite, so know each agent by dose, route, and signature toxicity. Deferoxamine, DFO, is parenteral, twenty-five to sixty milligrams per kilogram given subcutaneously or IV over eight to twelve hours, five days a week, with the shortest half-life of twenty to thirty minutes. Its classic toxicities are local injection reactions, ophthalmologic and auditory damage, and growth retardation in children. Deferiprone, DFP, is oral three times daily, dosed highest at seventy-five to one hundred milligrams per kilogram, and its board-favorite adverse effect is agranulocytosis in about zero point six percent, requiring weekly ANC monitoring, plus arthralgia in fifteen percent and zinc deficiency in about one percent. Deferasirox, DFX, is oral once daily, twenty to thirty milligrams per kilogram, with the longest half-life of eight to sixteen hours, excreted fecally, and its main issues are GI upset, rash, and a mild non-progressive creatinine rise. For chelation efficiency, deferasirox ranks highest at twenty-seven, deferoxamine thirteen, and deferiprone lowest at seven.
keypoints: DFO: SC/IV, 5 days/wk, short t½ (20-30min); toxicity = ophthalmologic/auditory, growth retardation
DFP: oral TID, highest dose (75-100mg/kg); agranulocytosis 0.6% → weekly ANC monitoring
DFX: oral once daily, longest t½ (8-16h), fecal excretion; watch for ↑creatinine
Chelation efficiency ranking: DFX(27) > DFO(13) > DFP(7)
keypoint_voiceover: Three chelators to memorize by their signature side effect: deferoxamine causes ophthalmologic and auditory toxicity plus growth retardation, and requires subcutaneous or IV infusion. Deferiprone's board answer is agranulocytosis, about zero point six percent, so it needs weekly neutrophil monitoring. Deferasirox is the once-daily oral option with the longest half-life, watch for a mild creatinine rise. And remember the efficiency ranking, deferasirox highest, then deferoxamine, then deferiprone lowest.
